newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia coffee lower, London seen declining.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia coffee lower, London seen declining.

text.p: Indonesian Robusta coffee prices were lower on Monday, with supply improving steadily despite the harvest peak being at least two months away.
Traders said the local price was quoted at 3,200-3,250 rupiah/kg in the key growing region of Lampung in South Sumatra, compared with 3,375-3,450 rupiah a week ago.
The export price was generally down to $1,400-$1,450/tonne FOB Lampung against $1,450-$1,500 last Monday, but quotes were also heard at up to $1,500.
The traders said they expected London coffee futures to open lower later on Monday, with May seen down $25-$30.
"The falls in New York prices for nearby months were likely to dampen sentiment at the opening in London," one trader said.

New York's most-active May fell 3.40 cents a lb last Friday to 165.75 cents, after the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) agreed at a technical committee meeting on Thursday in London to release an additional 200,000 bags of washed arabica coffee.
The meeting also decided to revoke an earlier export quota of 300,000 bags of arabica for the first half of 1997.
"I think the news has run its course and players will be looking at other factors," one local trader said.
"London and New York will be looking at the possible impact of the proposed truckers strike in Colombia," he said.

Colombia's main truckers association voted last Saturday to start an indefinite, nation-wide strike on April 20 to protest transport firms' failure to fulfil the terms of a deal hammered out to end a crippling 11-day truckers strike last October.
"It seems like there's more news for the arabica market," another local trader said. "Arabica supply is acknowledged to be tight, and this could squeeze it further."
On Indonesia, the trader said supply was improving but there were still expectations of lower production this year.
"My estimate is that production will be down by 10-15 percent this year," he said. "This is because of bad weather which affected the flowering process."
Local traders' expectations of lower output this year had generally been shrugged off by overseas' markets.
The Association of Indonesian Coffee Exporters expects 1996/97 (Oct/Sept) output to fall by 10 to 15 percent below its earlier forecast of 480,000 tonnes due to bad weather.
